title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 306
paragraphs: Hellenic customs they will by no means follow, and generally speaking they follow those of no other men whatever. This rule is observed by most of the Egyptians; but there is a large city named Chemmis in the Theban district near Neapolis, and in this city there is a temple of Perseus son of Danae, which is square-shaped, and around it grow date-palms. The gateway of the temple is built of stone and of very great size, and at the entrance two great stone statues stand. Within this enclosure is a temple-house, and in it stands an image of Perseus. These people of Chemmis say that Perseus often appears in their land and often within the temple, and that a sandal worn by him is sometimes found, measuring two cubits in length; and whenever this appears, all Egypt prospers. So they say, and they honour Perseus in Hellenic fashion thus: they hold an athletic contest, which includes the whole list of games, and they offer as prizes cattle, cloaks, and skins. When I asked why Perseus appeared to them alone, and why they were separated from all the other Egyptians in holding an athletic contest, they said that Perseus had been born of their city; for Danaus and Lynceus, they said, were men of Chemmis and had sailed to Hellas, and from them they traced a descent down to Perseus. They told me he had come to Egypt for the reason the Hellenes also give — namely to bring the Gorgon's head from Libya — and had then visited them too and recognised all his kinsfolk; and they said he had thoroughly learnt the name of Chemmis before coming to Egypt, since he had heard it from his mother, and that they celebrated an athletic contest for him by his own command.
